NEWS NOTES.
THE 14th O. N. G. has gone Niagara Falls for a ten days encampment.

THE Garfield Club at Steubenville, Ohio, numbers nearly 1,200 members.

GEN. DURBIN WARD was nominated for Congress in the Third Ohio District.

WILLIAM THOMAS of Pomeroy, was gored to death last week by an Alderney bull.

THE Democrats in some parts of Indiana are organizing Ku-Klux Klans, for the Presidential campaign.

GEN. JOHN C. FREMONT addressed a campaign club, in New York, on Wednesday of last week.

MCKINLEY, Gibson, Foster and Grosvenor, of Ohio, will take part in the campaign in Maine.

SENATOR MCDONALD admitted in an interview that he was surprised when English was nominated.

SECRETARY THOMPSON has been stirring up great enthusiasm among the Republicans of the Pacific Coast.

Of course New York and Indiana will both of them go Republican—for don't Jo. Blackburn say "he who doubts is damned."

SECRETARY SHERMAN will make his first speech of the campaign at Alexandria, Va., the latter part of this week.

The current tax assessment in Old Virginia, shows a decline in the taxable wealth of the State of from fifteen to twenty per cent.

The Democrats in Washington have "cheering intelligence" from Oregon. They had "cheering intelligence" from Oregon in 1877.

The National Democratic Committee will issue a campaign document of six hundred pages. Where is the mossback that will read it?

There is one thing about which all Democrats are agreed—that anything that tends towards keeping a Democrat out of office, is "unconstitutional."

GEN. HANCOCK said that the bayonet was not a fit instrument for collecting the votes of freemen. He didn't say anything about Southern ox-gads.

The Democrats have tried all kinds of soldiers upon their tickets, and failed. Let them try a statesman next time. Let them nominate Jeff. Davis.

A COLORED MAN at Danville, Ky., voted the Democratic ticket at the recent election. He had just been discharged from the Kentucky Penitentiary.

The campaign in the Solid South is opening up with the usual number of murders and whippings. Kentucky appears to be getting in most of the work.

GEN. GROSVENOR has issued a circular to the Republican of Athens County, which contains some excellent advice. The General wants "peace and victory."

GEN. CHALMERS says that Mississippi will this year give an increased Democratic majority. Gen. Chalmers is a Democrat, and represents, in Congress, a District having 13,000 Republican majority.

The Democratic headquarters at Washington are fitted up in splendid style—a leading Democrat remarking that it was time to dispel the idea that Democratic headquarters should consist of nothing but bed-bugs and empty whisky bottles.

GEN. GARFIELD's trip through New York last week, was a grand triumphal march. At every station he was greeted by cannon, music, banners, and immense crowds of people. It was a hearty greeting to the next President of the United States.

Some Spaniards attempted to get up a genuine Spanish Bull Fight in New York, last week, with a lot of sleepy Texas steers. The only success about the whole thing, was the success of the Sheriff in gobbling the receipts.

The Democrates are sending out thousands of copies of Garfield's "Salary-Grab Record," whatever that may be. We would not advise our Democratic friends to attempt to make the voters of their party believe that Garfield was a Salary Grabber. If successful, they will insure his election.
event-1880-08-2.A3:
BISMARCK, D. T., FRIDAY, AUG. 13, 1880. REPUBLICAN CONVENTION. A Republican Convention will be held at Vermillion, in the county of Clay, on Wednesday, Sept. 1, 1880, commencing at 1 p.m. for the purpose of placing in nomination a candidate for the office of Delegate in Congress from Dakota Territory. The ratio of representation will be one delegate for each 100 votes. or fraction over fifty, cast for Hon. G. G. Bennett at the general election of 1878, which will make the representation as follows, to-wit:
Armstrong . . . . . . . . . . .

THE greenback vote in Indiana this year inclines to the republicans, the democrats having refused to combine with them.

GEN. GARFIELD's trip to New York shows that the masses are in sympathy with him. He will surely receive the electoral vote of New York.

THE Leavenworth Times thinks that the solid south, now the corner stone of democratic hopes, is likely, after election, to become its grave stone.

THE Duluth Tribune remarks that the election in Alabama went democratic and that that is apt to be the case in states where none but democrats are allowed to vote.

MINNEHAHA and McCook counties have instructed their delegates to the territorial convention to vote for Pettigrew for congress. This gives him eleven votes for a starter.

Hancock objects to the bayonet as an implement for haryesting votes. The shotgun is generally used by democrats in the South for the purpose of gathering in the Republican vote, destroying or intimidating the voter.

During the last four years twenty-five United States officials have been murdered in the southern states while on duty, by men of the south opposed to recognizing the United States authority; yet it is proposed to surrender the control of the government to these people.

THE Michigan republicans, in their platform, call for a "free, unintimidated ballot and a fair count, with no tissue ballots or cipher dispatches." Hancock also makes some such remark in his letter of acceptance, but the republican votes cast in the south don't count all the same.

SOUTHERN Minnesota and Michigan mill men will send buyers to the North Pacific country for its extra No. 1 hard wheat to mix with the inferior grades raised in those regions. The North Pacific crop will amount to about 8,500,000 bushels, of which 5,000,000 bushels will be raised in Northern Dakota.

SOME vandal entered the Pioneer office at Deadwood recently, and after scattering and destroying considerable type, put in a line at the head of the paper announcing a new editor—J. Christ Donan—which run unnoticed through nearly the whole edition, very much to the disgust of the proprietor, Mr. Adams.

THE first wheat shipped from Northern Dakota to market this year will be from Bismuth, as the harvest here is ten days

earlier than in the Red River country; and the highest price paid will be at Bismarck because Bismarck has the advantage of water as well as rail transportation, and has flouring mills beside.

HANCOCK'S FREE BALLOT.

The campaign of the ku-klux in Indiana has begun. There are a few negroes in Muncie county, of that state, it appears, and the persons who give the blacks employment are receiving regular ku-klux warnings to dismiss them and "save trouble." The negroes themselves have also been notified to leave. This is a part of the process by which tue Hancock people intend to have a "free ballot" in the Hoosier state.—Minneapolis Tribune.

THE person writing the "Republican" article criticising the lecture of Chaplain McCabe, replies to THE TRIBUNE of last week. THE TRIBUNE will contribute ten dollars to the construction fund of Col. Bull's church if the Sun can show to Col. Bull's satisfaction that the writer of that article voted for either one of the republican presidents.

GRANT's order organizing the Boys in Blue for the campaign in Garfield's interest creates no little consternation in democratic ranks. The southern democrats profess to believe that the north under Grant is organizing for another war. As their military organizations, now semipolitical, are intended for war should occasion give opportunity to use arms, it is natural for them to believe the Boys in Blue are intended to represent the north on the tented field should an emergency arise.

WHERE REPUBLICAN VOTES ARE NOT COUNTED.

Of the late local election in Louisville, Ky., the Courier-Journal says: "It was both turbulent and corrupt. Money was used freely and openly, and, to the extent of their means, by all the candidates. There were a great number and variety of shindies; heads broken, noses mashed, eyes gouged, hair pulled, and, occasionally, a pistol shot and a knife thrust. On the whole, the day, though not tragical, was discreditable in the last degree. Demoralization ruled the roost, and rascals were rampant.

The worst blow received by Marshall Raymond in his campaign for the nomination for delegate, was that given by his old army comrade and friend, Major A. W. Edwards, of the Fargo Argus, who wrote up his fortune and princely ways of entertaining; and intimated that he was disposed to make a liberal use of "the stuff that makes the press turn easy" in order to attract the attention and gain the favor of the venal press. Now this wound given in the house of his friends is being torn open by such papers as the Deadwood Times, which pretend to be able to give the names of bummers to whom he has given various sums—in some instances $125 each—"just to please the boys."

Hancock talks of the glories of a free ballot, but a free ballot is unknown in the south, where his principal support comes from. No man can vote the republican ticket in the rebel states without being subject to persecution. Even the courts are converted into instruments for the oppression of republican voters. No Yankee gains respect in that country unless he has become a traitor to the cause for which the boys in blue fought. Hancock isn't respected. He is tolerated in the hope that through him the democratic party will gain power and through the democratic party the control of the government will pass into their hands, the rebel debt acknowledged and paid and the rebel soldiers pensioned. Most of the democratic party would not listen to any such schemes, but the south hopes for it as they hoped, for the democrats north to join them in the rebellion.
